title: Gurmukh and manmukh, deeper
hook: he paints the one facing the Guru and the one facing only the self

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true sati: not the one who burns on the pyre, but the one who lives in faithfulness. Your line was not the pyre. Who did you honor? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

Which way is your face pointed right now? Not your body. Your attention. Toward the phone, the worry, the next thing you want? Toward someone you love? It's a small question, and Guru Amar Das builds a great deal on it. Back near the start of this path, we met two words: gurmukh, the one facing the Guru, and manmukh, the one facing only their own mind. Today we go deeper, because in his hymns these aren't labels on a chart. He paints them, the way you'd paint two faces in the same crowded room.
screen: `WHICH WAY ARE YOU FACING?` → `TWO WORDS FROM THE START.` → `HE PAINTS THEM.`

segments.voice: Mukh means face. Gur-mukh, face toward the Guru. Man-mukh, face toward your own mind. Here are some of the strokes he uses, paraphrased from his hymns in Sri Rag and elsewhere. The manmukh is called blind, not because they can't see, but because they see only themselves. They act in ego and call it achievement. They read and recite, yet don't understand. They wander, and the wandering feels like freedom. The gurmukh, in his hymns, is at ease. Speaks sweetly. Sees the One light in everyone. Isn't shaken by praise or blame. Lives in the world but keeps the Name at the center. Now the deeper part. These aren't two kinds of people sorted at birth. They're two directions, and his hymns keep calling to the manmukh to turn. The same person can face the Guru at breakfast and face only themselves by lunch. That's why his language is so often about turning: the Word turns you around. In the Sikh view, you don't become a gurmukh by deciding you are one. You become one, again and again, by facing the Guru's teaching when the mind would rather face itself. It ties back to the start of his voice: ego and the Name can't share one room. Which of them gets the room depends on which way the face is turned. So the line today isn't a judgment on anyone. It's a direction: face the good.
screen: `MUKH: FACE.` · `BLIND, BECAUSE IT SEES ONLY ITSELF.` · `AT EASE, SEEING THE ONE IN ALL.` · `TWO DIRECTIONS, NOT TWO KINDS.` · then, large: `FACE THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn toward the good once. Settle, and let the breath slow. Notice where your attention is facing right now, without scolding yourself. A worry, a want, a screen. Then, slowly, turn it. Toward the breath. Toward someone you love. Toward a line of the Guru's Word you remember, like man too jot saroop hai. Let the turn be small and gentle. When the mind drifts back, that's fine; turning again is the practice. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out as you turn. The bell holds the time.
Gurmukh and manmukh. The one facing the Guru and the one facing only their own mind: in Guru Amar Das's hymns, two directions anyone can face. Today's word.
Your line: face the good. Today, once, when you notice your attention facing only yourself, turn it toward the good, and notice what changes. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Gurmukh and manmukh run through Guru Amar Das's hymns, which Sikhs hear in kirtan and katha; in Sikh teaching, becoming gurmukh is a lifelong turning toward the Guru's Word.

fork.setup: you notice you've spent the morning facing only your own wants. what do his hymns call for?
options: accept that you're a manmukh for good.
turn, through the Guru's Word, toward the Guru.
pretend you were a gurmukh all along.
fork.reveal: his hymns keep calling the manmukh to turn. it's a direction, so turning is always possible.

original.note: the one facing the Guru; set against the manmukh, facing only the self.

trapdoor: what you thought: gurmukh means a good Sikh, manmukh a bad one.
what it means: they're two directions of the face, and anyone can turn.
what a scholar hears: Guru Amar Das returns to the pair again and again, painting each with sharp images.
